EDR logs show a USB mass storage device attached to a Linux workstation performed a large sequential read across a specific range of sectors and then immediately overwrote those exact sectors with a uniform byte pattern. The device is an older portable music player recovered after a red-team test. What does this activity indicate and what are the first response steps?

<reasoning>The telemetry indicates a read of a contiguous block of sectors on the removable device followed within milliseconds by destructive writes to the identical locations. The firmware modification watches for reads targeting a particular sector window used by forensic imaging tools and responds by clearing the buffer or writing constant filler back to the media. Normal music playback or file copy operations perform scattered or sequential reads without then erasing the very sectors just read. Hardware faults also rarely produce such a perfectly targeted and immediately destructive pattern on a narrow range. The device type, the precise sector trigger, and the overwrite together eliminate ordinary user activity or benign driver behavior. This is the activation of a custom antiforensic capability intended to destroy evidence upon detection of imaging attempts.</reasoning>

A Linux endpoint executed a file that readelf reported as a standard shared library with normal DT_NEEDED entries, yet launching it directly caused an immediate shell to appear. The file arrived via a compromised web server. How is this possible and which telemetry fields would reveal the trick?

<reasoning>The execution path shows a single on-disk ELF producing two contradictory behaviors: one view of its program headers and dynamic table that the kernel accepts for mapping, and a second view that the dynamic linker uses to resolve a completely different library dependency that executes attacker code. The construction places two program header tables at different file offsets, adjusts the ELF header to point the kernel at one set and the linker at the other, then rewrites the string table entry for the first needed library. A compiler-generated shared object always presents identical load commands and symbol requirements to both the kernel loader and the runtime linker. The immediate shell without any of the normal library initialization or main routine flow further rules out a legitimate dlopen of a debugging library or a simple rename of an executable. The only coherent explanation is deliberate manipulation of the ELF metadata to exploit the differing parsers, achieving execution that evades simple static library dependency checks.</reasoning>
<answer>{"concept": "ELF parser differential between kernel execve loader and dynamic linker (ld.so)", "defender_friendly_explanation": "A crafted ELF file can embed two different program header tables and dynamic sections so the kernel maps one memory layout while the runtime linker resolves an entirely different set of libraries and entry points. The same file on disk therefore behaves as a benign library in some tools but executes malicious code when invoked directly.", "why_relevant_to_endpoint_defense": "EDR products and malware scanners that parse an ELF only once or trust a single loader view will classify the file as harmless. Attackers can drop the file through web shells or other initial access vectors and obtain execution that looks like ordinary library activity to basic analysis.", "key_telemetry_or_artifacts": ["Process creation events for files whose on-disk ELF header points to non-contiguous or duplicated program headers", "Image load or mmap events showing DT_NEEDED libraries that do not match the string table visible in the kernel view of the same file", "Binaries that are both marked executable and have valid shared-object headers being launched directly", "Unusual PT_PHDR or PT_DYNAMIC locations outside the first page or at offsets that differ between file and memory"], "mitre_techniques": ["T1055.001", "T1574.006", "T1036.005"], "suggested_hunt_or_detection": "Build or integrate a dual-parser ELF inspector in EDR that replays both the kernel program-header interpretation and the ld.so dynamic-section interpretation on every newly written executable or library, generating an alert on any mismatch in resolved dependencies or entry points."}</answer>

<reasoning>The question focuses on practical data sources for detecting ELF loader abuse involving duplicated or manipulated program headers and dynamic sections. Because the kernel and the dynamic linker perform different amounts of validation and different traversals of the on-disk structures, any telemetry that only records the final mapped memory or the final resolved libraries will miss the manipulation. I want to write a detection that catches binaries using IFUNC symbols or other dynamic linker metadata tricks to invoke sensitive libc functions without any obvious call instructions in the main code. What should the rule look for and how do I keep the false positive rate manageable?

<reasoning>The source material demonstrates how an attacker can place an IFUNC symbol in the dynamic section so that, when the linker resolves it, the resolver function is actually the address of a sensitive libc routine such as exit. The metadata alone causes the function to be invoked during symbol resolution without any normal call instruction appearing in the compiled code. A detection that only looks for suspicious strings or for explicit calls to system or exec will miss this entirely. The reliable signal is therefore the presence of an IFUNC-typed symbol whose resolver points at a high-value function, combined with the binary being executed from an unusual context. Because legitimate use of IFUNC is rare outside glibc internals and certain performance libraries, the pattern is highly diagnostic once the binary is not part of the base OS.</reasoning>
<answer>{"detection_title": "IFUNC resolver pointing to sensitive libc function in non-system ELF", "core_logic": "Alert when an ELF binary loaded from a user-writable or web-served location contains a dynamic symbol of type IFUNC whose resolver address, once the library base is applied, resolves to a sensitive function such as exit, system, or execve that is not part of the normal glibc IFUNC set for that architecture.", "primary_data_sources": ["File write events with full ELF header and dynamic section extraction", "Process creation events correlated with the image path", "Any available userland dynamic linker logging or eBPF trace of symbol resolution"], "mitre_techniques": ["T1055", "T1620"], "tuning_notes": "Exclude all files under /lib, /usr/lib, /lib64 and known compiler output paths. After a web shell compromise on a Linux box we recovered a binary that had been built with a custom makepoc-style tool. It had two different sets of program headers and a manipulated dynamic string table. Beyond basic process creation logs, what additional data sources or parsing steps would have given us early warning that this file was not a normal compiler output?

The key is therefore to inspect the raw ELF header fields and the layout of load segments at the moment the file is first written or first mapped for execution, rather than waiting for the process to run and only seeing the final memory image.</reasoning>
